candidates.title: Prompt2Echo (P2Echo): Text-Prompted Multi-View Echocardiography Segmentation with One Model
candidates.content: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. candidates.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
candidates.content: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. candidates.title: Embodied First Exam
candidates.content: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. candidates.title: Gemini Decisions API
candidates.content: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. candidates.title: RNA sequencing depth guidelines for the study of alternative splicing
candidates.content: Abstract A key parameter in the experimental design of RNA-seq projects is the choice of sequencing depth. Considering a limited budget, one needs to find a trade-off between the number of samples and the sensitivity of the analysis, particularly concerning lowly expressed genes. While previous studies have proposed a lower bound for the comprehensive analysis of differential gene expression, for the analysis of alternative splicing, it has only been proposed for human adipose tissue. However, alternative splicing differs across tissues and conditions. We analyzed publicly available and newly generated deep-sequenced paired-end RNA-seq samples (between 150 and >500 million reads, read length 50–150 bp) from human buffy coat cells and diverse sets of tissues, including gluteal subcutaneous fat, heart, and hypothalamus. Our results show that the sequencing depth typically used in published cohorts is not sufficient to comprehensively capture the landscape of alternative splicing. This motivates the use of deeper sequencing or long-read technologies in future studies. candidates.title: The balance between R-loops and RNAPII occupancy determines the outcome of transcription–replication conflicts
candidates.content: Abstract Maintaining genome integrity requires the precise coordination of replication and transcription. While R-loops are known to cause transcription–replication conflicts (TRCs), the precise nature of the barrier, whether it is the RNA:DNA hybrid itself, the stalled RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), or a combination of both, remains elusive. Using live-cell imaging in yeast to monitor a single R-loop prone locus in real time, we demonstrate that wild-type replisomes traverse R-loop enriched transcription units with high efficiency. We find that while R-loops initially repress transcription, replisome passage prompts a robust recovery of transcription activity. Indeed, we discover that R-loops serve a critical regulatory function by suppressing excessive RNAPII occupancy. In an RNAPII mutant with high DNA affinity, the enzymatic removal of R-loops leads to a pile-up of RNAPII molecules, creating a barrier to replication, more severe than the R-loops themselves. Thus, our findings reveal a dual nature of R-loops: while they can be obstacles and repress transcription, they can also serve as a physiological buffer that prevents the formation of high-density RNAPII ‘trains’. candidates.title: Truncated APC regulates alternative splicing by interacting with DDX21 in colorectal cancer
candidates.content: Abstract Truncating mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene—a key driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation—frequently lead to the production of a truncated APC protein (Trunc-APC). However, its post-transcriptional roles and oncogenic potential remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that Trunc-APC functions as an RNA-binding protein, directly associating with pre-mRNA via its N-terminal 1–169 amino acid region to regulate widespread alternative splicing (AS) in CRC cells. Specifically, Trunc-APC promotes exon inclusion in ARHGEF11 , producing an oncogenic isoform that is associated with enhanced Bcl-xL/BAX complex formation and reduced apoptosis. Mechanistically, Trunc-APC interacts with the RNA helicase DDX21 and facilitates SF3B complex recruitment to pre-mRNA, thereby modulating splicing patterns. Notably, treatment with the splicing inhibitor Madrasin significantly reduced tumor burden in ApcMin/+ CRC mice, indicating strong antitumor efficacy. candidates.title: A RARγ–SMARCA5 chromatin-remodeling axis stabilizes AR luminal programs and opposes lineage plasticity in prostate cancer
candidates.content: Abstract In prostate cancer (PCa), epigenomic mechanisms drive resistance to androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibitors, such as enzalutamide (enza). We tested whether retinoic acid receptor gamma (RARγ) shapes the epigenome to direct AR transcription, promote luminal identity, and limit enza resistance. RARγ restoration in enza-resistant 22Rv1 cells induced a large RARγ complex containing its coactivator TACC1 and the chromatin remodeler ISWI ATPase SMARCA5. RARγ restoration expanded and redistributed the AR cistrome toward active promoters, enhancers, and unique super-enhancers and increased the overlap with H3K27ac. RARγ restoration also increased SMARCA5 promoter-proximal binding that overlapped with G 2 /M-enriched AR cistrome, linking AR redistribution to cell cycle-associated chromatin engagement, including at luminal genes. In 22Rv1 and LNCaP C4-2 (also enza-resistant), RARγ restoration directed the AR transcriptome toward luminal differentiation. A miR-96 antagomir (targeting RARγ) mirrored the impact of RARγ restoration. candidates.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.13441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. candidates.content: arXiv:2611.13595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. Yet single-model accuracy remains insufficient for high-stakes use, and naive ensembling is vulnerable to systematic per-model biases that can drag aggregate accuracy below that of the strongest individual annotator. This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and G

candidates.title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.12998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear probes are a standard method to study geometric structures, such as helices and circles, from the activations of large language models (LLMs), and such structure is often taken as evidence that the model computes with it. Probe accuracy alone cannot establish this, because it conflates four separate claims. These are (1) that the concept is decodable from the activations, (2) that they form a specific shape, (3) that the shape belongs to the probed concept rather than to a related concept the model also represents, and (4) that the output of the model depends on the shape. We call these claims decodability, shape, ownership, and causal use, and we test them separately with a four-stage Bayesian pipeline. Stage 2 compares candidate shapes and selects the best one only when its evidence passes a predefined threshold. Stage 3 removes a set of related concepts, specified in advance, and tests whether the shape is owned or inherited. Stage 4 intervenes on the shape to test whether the output of the model depends on it. We apply the pipeline to two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Pythia 6.9B. candidates.content: arXiv:2611.13061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. candidates.title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.11306v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and $\texttt{robots.txt}$ directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and $\texttt{robots.txt}$, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. candidates.content: arXiv:2611.14174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the cross-border (XB) fulfillment center (FC) Selection Model: a multi-stage optimization framework combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to select optimal source FCs. For each source-destination shipping arc, the objective is to choose a subset of source-country FCs that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. We evaluate the model on three production-scale international shipping corridors for a large e-commerce company using 12 months of shipment data, employing both aggregate offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching. Across all shipping corridors, the XB FC Selection Model achieves 8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost relative to human expert-defined FC selection policies, with up to 6.5 percentage-point improvements in 5/5 target compliance (5 days, $5 USD). candidates.title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.13779v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature. On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task. The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents. Modeling and control require radically new approaches. candidates.title: TACT: Mitigating Overthinking and Overacting in Coding Agents via Activation Steering
candidates.content: arXiv:2605.05980v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When language model agents tackle complex software engineering tasks, they often degrade over long trajectories, which we define as *agent drift*. We focus on two recurring failure modes *overthinking* and *overacting*, i.e., where the agent repeatedly reasons over information it already has, and where it issues tool calls without integrating recent observations or acquiring new evidence. In this paper, we introduce TACT (Think-Act Calibration via activation Steering), to detect and mitigate agent drift in the residual stream before it surfaces as a behavioral failure. In specific, we label trajectory steps as overthinking, overacting, or calibrated, and find that their hidden states can separate linearly along two *drift axes*, pointing from calibrated behavior toward each failure mode (AUC $\approx$ 0.9). To mitigate agent drift, we project each step's activation onto these axes at test time and pull drifted ones back toward the calibrated region.
